history.heading: Early Japan
paragraphs: People have lived on the Japanese archipelago for at least 30,000 years. The Jōmon culture, which lasted from around 14,000 BCE to 300 BCE, produced some of the world's oldest known pottery. The Yayoi period that followed brought wet-rice farming, metalworking and new migrants from the Asian mainland.

By the 3rd to 7th centuries CE, powerful clans in the Yamato region had unified much of the country under a line of rulers from whom the present imperial family claims descent. Buddhism, Chinese writing and Chinese models of government arrived via Korea and China and reshaped the early state.

history.heading: Classical and feudal eras
paragraphs: The Nara (710–794) and Heian (794–1185) periods saw a refined court culture centred on the capitals of Nara and Kyoto, which produced works such as The Tale of Genji. Real power gradually shifted from the court to provincial warrior families.

From 1185 the country was led by shoguns, military rulers who governed in the emperor's name. Centuries of shifting power and civil war ended when Tokugawa Ieyasu founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603. For more than 250 years it kept internal peace and sharply limited contact with the outside world.

history.heading: Meiji modernisation and empire
paragraphs: After US warships forced Japan to open its ports in 1853–54, the shogunate collapsed and the Meiji Restoration of 1868 returned formal authority to the emperor. Japan industrialised at remarkable speed, adopting a constitution, a modern army and Western-style institutions.

Japan defeated China (1894–95) and Russia (1904–05) and colonised Taiwan and Korea. Expansion into Manchuria and a full-scale war with China from 1937 led to the Pacific War against the United States and its allies. The war ended in 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, with Japan devastated and occupied.

history.heading: Postwar Japan
paragraphs: Under US-led occupation, Japan adopted a new constitution in 1947 that made the emperor a symbol of the state and renounced war. The following decades brought an "economic miracle" that made Japan the world's second-largest economy by the late 1960s.

An asset bubble burst in the early 1990s, leading to a long period of slow growth often called the "Lost Decades". The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima nuclear disaster were a major national trauma. Today Japan faces a rapidly ageing and shrinking population.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Japanese is spoken by nearly the entire population. It is written with a mix of kanji (characters adapted from Chinese) and two native syllabaries, hiragana and katakana. Ainu and the Ryukyuan languages are indigenous minority languages, all of them endangered.

Most Japanese people take part in both Shinto and Buddhist practices without seeing them as exclusive: Shinto shrines are visited for births, New Year and festivals, while Buddhist rites are common for funerals and remembering ancestors. Many people describe themselves as not religious.

culture.heading: Arts and aesthetics
paragraphs: Traditional arts include the theatre forms of noh and kabuki, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, calligraphy, the tea ceremony and ikebana flower arranging. Ideas such as wabi-sabi, the beauty of the imperfect and transient, have influenced design far beyond Japan.

Modern Japanese culture has a huge global reach through anime, manga, video games, film and fashion. Directors such as Akira Kurosawa and Hayao Miyazaki and companies such as Nintendo are known worldwide.

culture.heading: Food
paragraphs: Japanese cuisine, recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2013, emphasises seasonal ingredients and careful presentation. Rice, fish, soy, seaweed and fermented foods such as miso are staples.

Well-known dishes include sushi, sashimi, ramen, tempura, soba and udon noodles, and regional specialities from every prefecture. Eating out is an important part of social life, from small izakaya pubs to highly rated restaurants.

culture.heading: Customs and sport
paragraphs: Social life places weight on politeness, harmony within the group and reading context. Bowing, gift-giving and seasonal events such as cherry-blossom viewing (hanami) and the summer Obon festival are widely observed.

Sumo is the traditional national sport, and martial arts such as judo, karate and kendo originated in Japan. Baseball is the most popular team sport, and football has grown strongly since the 1990s. Tokyo hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964 and 2021.

politics.heading: System of government
paragraphs: Japan is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system. The emperor is "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people" and has no political powers. The current emperor, Naruhito, came to the throne in 2019.

Legislative power belongs to the National Diet, made up of the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors. The prime minister is chosen by the Diet, is usually the leader of the largest party in the lower house, and leads the cabinet.

politics.heading: Parties and political life
paragraphs: The conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) has governed for almost the entire period since its founding in 1955, usually in coalition, with brief opposition-led governments in 1993–94 and 2009–12. The opposition has often been fragmented between several centre-left and reformist parties.
Long-running debates include whether to revise the pacifist Article 9 of the constitution, how to respond to the ageing population, immigration policy and the future of nuclear power.

politics.heading: Defence and foreign relations
paragraphs: Japan's armed forces are officially the Self-Defense Forces. The alliance with the United States, under a 1960 security treaty, is the cornerstone of its security policy, and US forces are stationed in Japan, especially in Okinawa.

Japan is a member of the G7 and a major aid donor. Relations with China and South Korea are shaped by trade ties as well as wartime history and territorial disputes. Japan has unresolved territorial disputes with Russia over the southern Kuril Islands, with South Korea over the Liancourt Rocks, and with China over the Senkaku Islands.

economy.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Japan has one of the world's largest economies and is a highly developed, high-income country. It is a world leader in cars, electronics, machinery, robotics and materials, home to firms such as Toyota, Sony and Panasonic.
The currency is the yen (¥), one of the world's main reserve currencies. The Bank of Japan kept interest rates at or below zero for many years to fight deflation, and began raising them in 2024.

economy.heading: Industry and trade
paragraphs: Manufacturing is concentrated along the Pacific coast between Tokyo and Osaka. Japanese companies have built large production networks across Asia and North America. Services, including finance, retail and a fast-growing tourism sector, now make up most of the economy.

Because Japan has few natural resources, it imports most of its energy, food and raw materials. Its main trading partners are China, the United States and other Asian economies, and it belongs to free-trade agreements including the CPTPP and RCEP.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Japan's population has been shrinking since around 2010 and has one of the highest shares of older people in the world, which creates labour shortages and puts pressure on pensions and healthcare. Public debt is among the highest of any developed economy, at over twice the size of GDP, although most of it is held domestically.
Policy responses include encouraging more women and older people to work, accepting more foreign workers, automation, and efforts to raise wages and productivity.
